mcqs.question: What's the correct rule for choosing between a local and a distributed cache?
options: Always use a distributed cache since it's more consistent in every case
Local cache for data tolerant of per-node inconsistency that needs sub-millisecond access; distributed cache for shared state every node must agree on
Always use a local cache since it's faster in every case
The choice between local and distributed caching has no measurable effect on latency
mcqs.explanation: The decision hinges on whether nodes can disagree without causing harm — if yes and speed matters most, local wins; if every node must see the same value, distributed wins. Defaulting to either extreme ignores the actual trade-off, and the latency difference between the two is large enough (often orders of magnitude) to matter for a hot code path.

mcqs.question: What's the actual benefit of a two-tier cache with a small local cache in front of a distributed one?
options: It eliminates the need for a distributed cache entirely once the local tier is in place
It guarantees every node always has an identical view of the data
The local tier absorbs traffic for the hottest keys before it ever reaches the network, while the distributed cache remains the shared, consistent source for everything else
It only works if the distributed cache is disabled during peak traffic
mcqs.explanation: The two tiers do different jobs: local soaks up the highest-traffic keys with sub-microsecond speed, and distributed still backs everything with a shared, consistent copy for keys the local tier doesn't hold. It doesn't remove the need for the distributed cache — it complements it — and it doesn't magically make every node's local view identical, which is exactly the trade-off local caching carries.

mcqs.question: How do you invalidate a local, in-process cache across every node when the underlying data changes?
options: Restart every node whenever the underlying data changes
Increase the local cache's size so stale entries are evicted faster on their own
Route all writes through a single node so the local caches never have a chance to diverge
Publish an invalidation event on a pub/sub channel that every node subscribes to and clears its own local copy on, backed by a TTL in case a node misses the message
mcqs.explanation: Since there's no single delete call that reaches every node's memory, an event-driven approach — pub/sub plus a TTL backstop for missed messages — is the practical fix, mirroring event-driven invalidation applied to N independent local caches. Restarting nodes on every change is disruptive and unscalable, a bigger cache doesn't cause faster eviction of specifically stale entries, and routing all writes through one node doesn't address that the change still needs to reach every other node's local copy.

mcqs.question: A team assumes their existing Redis cache is "fast enough" for any caching need in the system. What's the flaw?
options: A network round trip, even to a fast in-memory store, is orders of magnitude slower than an in-process lookup — for a hot path called on every request, that gap can dominate total latency
Redis is never fast enough for any production workload
This only matters for workloads handling more than a million requests per second
Local caches are always strictly better than distributed caches in every scenario
mcqs.explanation: Even a sub-millisecond Redis response is roughly a thousand times slower than an in-process memory lookup — for a code path hit on every request, that difference can be the dominant cost, regardless of how well-tuned Redis is. Redis is genuinely fast enough for plenty of workloads, this isn't gated to extreme request volumes, and local caches carry their own real costs (memory multiplication, harder invalidation) that make them not universally better.
